topics.title: Introduction to Force
topics.content: Force is a physical cause that changes the state of rest or motion of a body. SI unit is Newton (N), CGS unit is Dyne. 1 Newton = 10^5 dyne. Two types: Contact forces (friction, tension, normal) and Non-contact forces (gravity, magnetic, electric).

question.prompt: What is the SI unit of force?
question.explanation: The SI unit of force is Newton (N). 1 N = 10^5 dyne.

topics.title: Newton's First Law - Law of Inertia
topics.content: A body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless an external force acts on it. This is also called the Law of Inertia. Examples: passenger lurching forward when bus stops, tablecloth trick, spacecraft moving in space without friction.

question.prompt: A bus suddenly stops. Passengers lurch forward because of:
question.hint: Objects in motion tend to stay in motion...
question.explanation: Due to inertia, passengers maintain their forward motion even when the bus stops.

topics.title: Newton's Second Law - F=ma
topics.content: The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force. F = dp/dt = m × dv/dt = m × a, therefore F = ma. Force is measured in Newtons when mass is in kg and acceleration in m/s².

question.prompt: A 5 kg object accelerates at 3 m/s². What force is applied?

topics.title: Newton's Third Law - Action and Reaction
topics.content: To every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. F₁₂ = -F₂₁. The action and reaction forces act on DIFFERENT bodies. Examples: rocket propulsion (gases push rocket up, rocket pushes gases down), walking (you push ground back, ground pushes you forward).

question.prompt: A rocket moves up by pushing gases down. This demonstrates:
question.explanation: Rocket pushes gases down (action), gases push rocket up (reaction). Classic example of Newton's Third Law.

topics.title: Momentum
topics.content: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity: p = mv. It is a vector quantity (has direction). SI unit is kg·m/s. Conservation of momentum: In an isolated system, total momentum before = total momentum after collision.

question.prompt: Calculate momentum: 2 kg ball moving at 10 m/s.

topics.title: Equations of Motion
topics.content: Three kinematic equations: (1) v = u + at, (2) s = ut + ½at², (3) v² = u² + 2as. Where u = initial velocity, v = final velocity, a = acceleration, t = time, s = displacement. Use equation 3 when time is not given.

question.prompt: Which equation relates velocity, displacement, and acceleration (no time)?
question.hint: Look for the one WITHOUT time (t)
question.explanation: v² = u² + 2as is the only equation that doesn't contain time (t).

topics.title: Moment of Force (Torque)
topics.content: Moment of force (torque) is the turning effect of a force about a pivot. τ = F × d, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot. SI unit: Nm. Clockwise moments are negative, anticlockwise are positive.

question.prompt: A 20N force acts 0.5m from pivot. What is the moment?

topics.title: Equilibrium of Bodies
topics.content: A body is in equilibrium when net force = 0 AND net moment = 0. Static equilibrium: body at rest. Dynamic equilibrium: body in uniform motion. Principle of moments: sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments.

question.prompt: A book resting on a table is in which type of equilibrium?
question.hint: Is it moving or at rest?
question.explanation: Static equilibrium = at rest with net force = 0.

topics.title: Centre of Gravity
topics.content: Centre of Gravity (C.G.) is the point where the entire weight of a body appears to act. For regular shapes: Ring/Circle - center, Triangle - centroid (1/3 from base), Rectangle - intersection of diagonals, Rod - midpoint.

question.prompt: Where is the Centre of Gravity of a uniform ring?
question.explanation: For a ring, the C.G. is at the geometric center, which is empty space!

topics.title: Uniform Circular Motion
topics.content: Object moving in circle at constant speed. Direction of velocity changes, so it's accelerated motion. Centripetal force points towards center (real force). Centrifugal force points away from center (fictitious/pseudo force - not real!).

question.prompt: Centrifugal force is a real force.
question.hint: Is it a real force or just an apparent one?
question.explanation: Centrifugal force is FICTITIOUS (pseudo force). Only centripetal force is real!
